result:
Two branches share no common ancestor commit → git has no merge base, refuses by default (since 2.9) to avoid accidentally mashing two separate projects together.

Usual cause: `git init` + commit locally, then `git pull` from a remote that was created with its own initial commit (README/license). Others: wrong remote URL, history rewritten on one side (rebase/filter-repo/force-push), a shallow clone, or an orphan branch.

Check the remote is the right repo first (`git remote -v`). If it is, and you do want both histories combined:

```
git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories
```

(or `git merge <branch> --allow-unrelated-histories`). Resolve conflicts, typically README/.gitignore, then commit.

If your local repo has nothing worth keeping, re-cloning is simpler. If the remote only has an auto-generated README you don't care about, `git push --force` overwrites it; this destroys the remote history, so use it only on a repo nobody else uses.

If the histories are unrelated because someone rewrote the remote, don't merge: you'd resurrect the old history. Back up your work and reset to or re-clone the new one.
